analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $4.65 in steps through 1992.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed a minimum wage increase 62-37 on April 12, 1989, but did it through a companion bill, H.R. 2, instead of S. 4; the law finally enacted stopped at $4.25 an hour rather than the $4.65 S. 4 proposed.
analysis.plain_summary: S. 4 would have raised the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.85 in 1990, $4.25 in 1991, and $4.65 in 1992 and after [S2][S4]. It also raised the sales threshold that exempts some small retail and service businesses from federal wage rules, set a special, slower schedule for Puerto Rico, and let employers count a bigger share of tips toward the minimum wage for tipped workers [S2][S3]. The Senate debated it in April 1989, defeated an attempt to send it back to committee, then passed the increase through a companion bill instead; the increase that became law topped out at $4.25, and S. 4 itself was indefinitely postponed the next January [S6][S7][S8].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, most of them in retail, restaurants, and other low-wage service jobs, who would see their hourly pay rise by up to $1.30 over three years [S2][S4]. Some small businesses with less than $500,000 in annual sales gain an exemption from federal wage coverage, though businesses already covered must keep paying the $3.35 floor [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid the federal minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.85 in 1990, $4.25 in 1991, and $4.65 in 1992 and thereafter, restoring much of the ground the wage floor lost to inflation during the 1980s.
Keeps overtime and child labor protections in place for workers at newly exempted small businesses, and keeps a $3.35 wage floor for businesses that were covered in 1988.

Retains federal minimum wage coverage in Puerto Rico with a floor of $3.35 an hour while phasing in the full federal rate for lower-wage Puerto Rico industries gradually, reaching the full rate between 1994 and 1996 depending on the industry.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — retail stores, restaurants, and small service businesses — who face higher payroll costs, some of which may be passed to customers through prices. Restaurants employing tipped workers get part of that offset through a larger tip credit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The reported bill raises the tip credit from 40 percent to 45 percent in 1990 and 50 percent thereafter, letting employers count tips against half the minimum wage and reducing the guaranteed cash wage employers must pay tipped workers directly.

Raising the small-business exemption threshold to $500,000 in annual sales removes some retail and service establishments from federal minimum wage, overtime, and child labor coverage, though businesses covered in 1988 must keep paying at least $3.35.
Employers in Puerto Rico and lower-wage territory industries get multi-year phase-ins, delaying the full federal rate there until as late as 1996 for some government employees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a higher wage floor for millions of low-paid workers versus higher labor costs for the businesses that employ them, partially cushioned by a bigger small-business exemption, a larger tip credit, and longer phase-ins for Puerto Rico. Those cushioning provisions are real concessions that reduce what low-wage employers pay, especially for tipped workers, and the version that finally passed dropped the bill's $4.65 endpoint entirely — so the honest reading is that the help for workers was real but smaller than what was introduced.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate debated S. 4 in April 1989, beat back a 43-56 vote to send it back to committee, then passed the same minimum wage increase through a companion House bill in lieu of S. 4; the increase that finally became law stopped at $4.25 an hour instead of $4.65, and S. 4 itself was indefinitely postponed by unanimous consent in January 1990.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced S. 4 on January 25, 1989, and it was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which he chaired.

The committee held hearings on March 3, ordered the bill reported on March 8, and reported it on March 13 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and minority views filed, placing it on the Senate calendar.
On April 12, 1989, the Senate rejected a motion to recommit the bill to committee by 43-56, with 40 of 45 Republicans voting to send it back and only 3 of 55 Democrats.
The Senate then incorporated S. 4 into H.R. 2 as an amendment and passed H.R. 2 in lieu of S. 4 by 62-37, with 52 of 55 Democrats voting yes and only 10 of 45 Republicans.
S. 4 was indefinitely postponed by unanimous consent on January 24, 1990, ending the bill in its original form.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Minimum-wage workers won a real raise, but the law enacted topped out at $4.25 rather than S. 4's $4.65, so low-wage employers — restaurants above all, which kept a larger tip credit — came out ahead relative to what was originally proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers, who avoided the $4.65 rate

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA); Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 4, held committee hearings, and reported it to the Senate with an amendment on March 13, 1989.

for.name: George Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Joined Kennedy in introducing the bill as an original cosponsor.

for.name: 52 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage of the minimum wage increase via H.R. 2.

against.name: 40 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted yes on the motion to recommit the bill to committee, a move to keep it from advancing; the motion failed 43-56.

against.name: 35 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage of the minimum wage increase.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising the minimum wage as high as S. 4 proposed, backed a smaller increase, and signed the final compromise that stopped at $4.25 with a training subminimum.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed the increase almost unanimously (52-2 on passage, 51-3 against recommittal) while most Republicans opposed it (35 of 45 voted no on passage; 40 of 45 voted to recommit), with 10 Republicans joining final passage.

industries.note: A higher wage floor directly raises their payroll costs, and their interest ran against the wage increase their employees would receive. The bill did cushion them with a larger small-business exemption.
They face a higher wage floor, but the reported bill raised the tip credit to 50 percent, letting tips cover half the minimum wage and reducing the cash employers must pay tipped workers directly.

industries.industry: Small businesses under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: Newly exempt establishments escape federal wage, overtime, and child labor rules; businesses already covered in 1988 must keep paying at least $3.35.
They face eventual increases but win long gradual phase-ins, with the full federal rate arriving between 1994 and 1996 for lower-wage industries, and a $3.35 floor under wage orders.
